newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentine unions fail to impress with tepid strike.
newsitem.headline: Argentine unions fail to impress with tepid strike.

text.p: Argentina's unions were pondering their next move on Friday after a patchy 24-hour general strike that apparently failed to impress a government determined to push on with free market labour changes.

Thursday's stoppage interrupted public transport in Buenos Aires, filling the capital with traffic jams as white collar employees took their own cars to work. It stopped half the industry in Buenos Aires and more in the provincial centres of Rosario and Tucuman. But most shops and banks worked as normal.

A relieved government said it estimated only 28 percent of workers around the country joined in the third general strike called by the CGT labour federation since August. "The CGT did not manage to explain the reasons for the strike to the people," Social Security Secretary Carlos Torres said on Friday of the stoppage called to protest decrees imposing labour market changes.

CGT chief Rodolfo Daer said at least 83 percent of Argentines stayed away from work but truck drivers union boss Hugo Moyano admitted the strike was not as big as the last one in September. Moyano, who recently withdrew from the CGT's leadership, said Argentina's already divided labour movement could fracture still further unless the federation gritted its teeth and adopted a consistant hard line with the government.

"If we start all this coming and going again, like saying it's going to be a hot summer but that we don't want to end the dialogue with the government, then obviously the labour federation will break up," he told local radio.

The CGT called its third strike this year after President Carlos Menem lost patience last week with talks with the unions to hammer out a compromise over laws to cut employers' costs and make Argentine labour markets more flexible. Menem imposed the laws by decree, leading the CGT to call a 24-hour stoppage in August and the September strike.

The size of the 36-hour September stoppage surprised the government and gave new credibility to a union movement that leftwingers accuse of being too close to the government. The CGT is dominated by the governing Peronist Party and had been reluctant to wield more than harsh words against Menem.

But even the September strike failed to win more than a place at a negotiating table. The government refused to back down on plans to cut union negotiating power, whittle away at its health care monopoly and make working hours more flexible.
CGT chief spokesman Carlos West Ocampo said on Friday more strikes might come. "It will be analysed this afternoon by the CGT council and next Monday," he said.
The government, which has said it plans more labour decrees, hopes a more flexible employment market will help reduce Argentina's 17.3 percent unemployment rate.
